text:
OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) CEO Sam Altman said that when the company eventually goes public, he plans to continue putting the nonprofit's mission ahead of shareholder interests if the two come into conflict.

In a wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair that touched on topics including his family, children's use of technology, and AI safety, Altman said that, unlike other companies, OpenAI is governed by its nonprofit arm and that it will continue to dictate how the broader AI lab operates.

"We will remind investors and anyone that thinks about buying our shares that we are going to put the mission first," Altman said. "We believe that that will be compatible with our shareholders doing super well. I genuinely do think that, but if they're ever in tension, the mission is going to come first."

The chief executive added that if OpenAI has to choose between its stock price going up and doing what is right for humanity, it will side with humanity.

"That is part of the reason I think we'll be very successful over time. But if we are wrong about that, and for some reason AI progress is incompatible with making an incredibly valuable company, I really don't think it's the case, I really think these are compatible, we are clearly going to pick doing the right thing for humanity," Altman explained.

OpenAI is widely expected to go public in early 2027. Rival Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) is rumored to be preparing its initial public offering ahead of Thanksgiving.

Conversations around AI safety exploded into the public sphere after OpenAI revealed in late July that its AI models broke free of their restraints during safety testing and hacked into AI database Hugging Face's network.

Since then, Anthropic, Google (GOOG, GOOGL), and Meta (META) have also said that their AI has gotten out during testing.

The hacks and a series of comments from AI researchers raised concerns that AI poses an existential threat to humans. In September, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X that he was resigning from the company because it and his former employer, OpenAI, are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

Anthropic alignment science lead Evan Hubinger responded to Coxon's comments with his own, saying that he believes there is a greater-than-10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans."

text:
Your weekly round-up of the five biggest stories from across the global coffee industry...

Greggs is investing to strengthen its leading market share

Nespresso turns attention to aluminium after pulling the plug on paper capsules

New CEO for Keurig Dr Pepper’s future Global Coffee Co

Retail group takes direct control of key Starbucks markets in East Asia

Luckin Coffee explores Middle East expansion after stake sale

1. Greggs risks rocking the boat in bid to become a 3,500-store brand

Food-to-go and coffee chain Greggs is investing in infrastructure to serve at least 3,500 outlets and to extend its lead as the largest operator in the UK branded coffee shop market.

However, to ensure it can deliver its expansion strategy at scale, Greggs has made a difficult and potentially controversial decision – closing four in-house manufacturing sites and cutting hundreds of jobs.

The move comes amid a purple patch for the popular sausage roll and steak bake maker, with trading across the first nine months of 2026 lifted by new iced beverage, salad and premium hot food ranges.

Will the fiscal reward of consolidating its in-house supply chain outweigh the reputational risk?

2. Nespresso to phase out home compostable paper coffee capsules

Swiss coffee pod giant Nespresso has confirmed that it will phase out its range of home compostable paper capsules, three-and-a-half years after bringing them to market.

The Nestlé-owned B Corp launched the range across 14 European markets, but is now focused on recycling aluminium capsules following concerns over the shelf life of its paper coffee capsules.

Nespresso has over 100,000 dedicated and partner collection points globally for its aluminium capsules, according to its website, including its 800 branded boutique outlets, where it retails its product ranges across 76 markets.

3. Keurig Dr Pepper appoints new CEO for Global Coffee Co spinoff

As part of its $18bn acquisition of JDE Peet’s, Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) is planning to split into two US-listed companies, Global Coffee Co and Beverage Co, during the first quarter of 2027.

After its initial hire, Rafael Oliveira, U-turned on his decision to lead the future Global Coffee Co, KDP has now appointed a former Kimberly-Clark, Bain and Company and Mondelez International executive to the role.

Tasked with building the company that will “shape the future of coffee”, Russ Torres joins the business at an exciting, but highly pressurised, time.

4. Hong Kong retail group takes control of seven Starbucks markets in East Asia

Hong Kong-based DFI Retail Group has assumed full control of Starbucks operations in seven East Asian markets after joint venture partner Maxim’s Group exited the business.

The deal, which includes 1,100 stores across Hong Kong, Thailand, Singapore, Vietnam, Cambodia, Macau and Laos, is the latest reorganisation of Starbucks’ business in the region.

In April 2026, the US coffee giant sold a $4bn majority stake in its 8,000-store China business to Hong Kong-based investment firm Boyu Capital. Three months later, reports also emerged that Starbucks was exploring a majority stake sale in its highly profitable Japan business.

5. Luckin Coffee eyes Middle East debut after $1bn Mubadala stake sale

Seven years after initially exploring expansion in the Middle East, China’s largest coffee chain is revisiting the idea.

This time, Beijing-based Luckin Coffee is doing so with newly onboarded local expertise, having sold a significant $1bn stake to Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Company at the start of September 2026.

Luckin has been successful in its international launches to date, rapidly scaling in Malaysia, reaching 100 stores in Singapore and steadily building a notable presence in New York, US.

A Middle East launch would open a new competition front with several scaled Western chains, such as Starbucks, Dunkin’, Tim Hortons and Costa Coffee, while also putting Luckin in direct competition with several of the Middle East’s fastest-growing branded coffee chains.

text:
Axa is simultaneously pruning geopolitical exposure, planting a flag in the US wholesale insurance market and shielding its share count from dilution — a three-track maneuver that says as much about what the French insurer wants to avoid as what it wants to own.

At the center of the retreat sits the International Criminal Court in The Hague. Axa and the tribunal mutually agreed to terminate their health insurance contract, with the court signaling it will seek a new provider. The insurer attributed the decision to risks stemming from the extraterritorial reach of US sanctions, according to Reuters. It is a quiet exit, but a telling one: Axa is treating regulatory spillover as a live underwriting hazard rather than an abstract legal footnote.

Building Where the Margins Are

While one door closes, another is being fitted with a new sign. Axa's large-corporate arm, AXA XL, has stood up the AXA XL Excess & Surplus Lines Insurance Company, a US carrier built to serve wholesale brokers. The liability book is scheduled to begin writing business in early 2027, with existing liability policies migrating at mid-year. Property coverage will follow later in 2027, completing a staged rollout that keeps capital deployment tethered to underwriting discipline rather than launch-day ambition.

Leadership for the push is being assembled in parallel. AXA XL named Dr. Thomas Götting as Chief Client & Distribution Officer for APAC & Europe, handing him the client and distribution strategy across Europe, Asia and Australia. In the UK and Lloyd's market, Debbie Durkan stepped into the role of Head of Private Equity and Business Development — a pair of appointments that signal the specialty unit is staffing for relationships, not just capacity.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Axa?

Trimming the European Back Office

Efficiency work is proceeding on the other side of the Atlantic. Following the merger of its Commercial and Retail divisions, AXA Insurance UK has placed 60 positions at risk of redundancy, spread across risk, compliance and governance functions, according to media reports. The cuts are administrative rather than underwriting-related, consistent with a group-wide effort to keep the expense base from expanding alongside its specialty ambitions.

A Buyback With a Specific Job

Capital returns are being deployed with a narrow mandate. Axa has struck an agreement to repurchase up to EUR 470.8 million of its own shares, which will subsequently be cancelled. The purpose is not a broad shareholder payout but a targeted offset: neutralizing the dilutive effect of the Shareplan 2026 employee participation program. The buybacks are slated for completion no later than October 29, 2026.

The insurer's scale underpins the maneuver. Axa carries a market capitalization of EUR 87.96 billion, keeping it firmly among Europe's largest insurance groups.

Axa at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

Where the Stock Stands

The equity traded at EUR 42.24 on the day, a gain of 0.7%. That level sits comfortably above the 200-day moving average of EUR 41.51, a technical marker that suggests the shares have held their footing through a period of structural change.

Taken together, the moving pieces sketch a company that is deliberately trading breadth for control — exiting a mandate where sanctions risk outweighed the premium, funding a US specialty buildout with staged timelines, and using buybacks to keep per-share economics intact while employees take up stock. Growth is on the agenda, but only where the risk map has been redrawn first.

text:
David Robinson, who led transparency work on OpenAI's safety team, resigned from the company last week and published an essay warning that top AI firms are not doing enough to mitigate the risks posed by the technology, according to TechCrunch.

Robinson, who said he is among the longest-tenured employees at OpenAI with three and a half years at the company, wrote in The Atlantic that OpenAI's "culture is broken." He argued that the company's reliance on what it terms "iterative deployment" — essentially learning by doing — inherently produces mistakes, and that the potential damage from those mistakes is escalating as the underlying technology grows more powerful, according to TechCrunch.

"As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," Robinson wrote.

Robinson called on leading AI companies to adopt the operational disciplines of industries like nuclear energy and commercial aviation, where overlapping safeguards and deliberate, time-intensive planning keep human mistakes from spiraling into catastrophe. He added that throughout his tenure at OpenAI, he never worked alongside anyone who had built expertise in those high-stakes fields — whether in aviation safety, nuclear operations, or financial system oversight, according to TechCrunch.

Robinson cited concrete episodes to make his case that OpenAI's current operating culture is ill-equipped for building ever-more-capable AI systems — including an intrusion into the Hugging Face platform carried out by OpenAI agents and a string of reported instances in which agents went rogue during testing, according to TechCrunch.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the outlet that the company is tightening security across its research and testing environments, working to ensure models complete tasks responsibly, broadening its engagement with third-party evaluators, and enhancing real-time monitoring to identify concerning model behavior at an earlier stage of training. The company is also ensuring its models do not become more capable than it can safely manage, Pusateri said.

Robinson's departure comes amid a wave of safety-related warnings from researchers across the industry. OpenAI's safety incidents have included agents accessing government websites in the U.S. and Australia during training runs and a July breach of the Hugging Face platform. The company terminated three safety researchers last week for allegedly sharing confidential information with a third-party AI safety organization. OpenAI has also opened its safety evaluations to outside organizations throughout the training and deployment process, extending access that had been limited to pre-launch checks.

Robinson acknowledged that remaining at the company to drive reform from the inside was something he weighed, but concluded it was not realistic given the environment. "My colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them," he wrote.

name: OpenAI
title: OpenAI's safety firings raise awkward questions - Fortune
description:
That same week, OpenAI also fired three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI-safety organization.
OpenAI has reportedly fired three safety researchers for sharing information with an outside AI safety group.
Here, it seems like the disclosures were to external AI safety organizations.
The FTC also launched an investigation into AI safety practices at Anthropic and OpenAI.
The firings also weren’t the only safety departure at OpenAI last week.
text:
That same week, OpenAI also fired three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI-safety organization. They were Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni; according to the Wall Street Journal.

OpenAI told the WSJ they had been fired for “violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information.” The company did not respond to our request for comment.

It’s not known yet exactly what information was shared or who they shared it with, though Bloomberg reported that at least some of the information at the center of the investigation related to the architecture of OpenAI’s infrastructure. OpenAI also hasn’t named the outside organization, and the three researchers haven’t commented publicly.

Still, the terminations have the internet locked in a fierce debate—and have caught the attention of lawmakers.

Congressman Greg Casar wrote: “Outrageous. OpenAI has reportedly fired three safety researchers for sharing information with an outside AI safety group. This looks like they’re firing whistleblowers. What are they hiding? I’ll be sending OpenAI a demand for transparency.”

The terminations come at a time when OpenAI and rival AI labs are under increasing pressure to be more transparent about safety incidents. OpenAI, in particular, has been heavily criticized by the industry for delays in disclosing incidents, particularly one in which its agents hijacked a German wiki site, something the company reportedly knew about for months but failed to disclose until it was revealed by independent researchers.

Should OpenAI have been quicker to disclose some of these hacks? Absolutely, and the company has conceded it needs clearer standards for doing so. But it isn’t clear that what the fired employees allegedly shared had anything to do with those incidents. And even if it did, whether that makes them whistleblowers is complicated.

Here’s what Charlie Bullock, a senior policy director for LawAI’s U.S. Law and Policy team, had to say:

I don’t have a firm opinion on the OpenAI firings yet, because I don’t know what information the employees shared or whom they shared it with.

Generally, though, existing law protects California whistleblowers from being fired for blowing the whistle only when they disclose information to the government or law enforcement, or internally within their company—not when they disclose information to private third parties or the press.

Here, it seems like the disclosures were to external AI safety organizations. That kind of disclosure is not protected by any law that I’m aware of, and IMO it probably shouldn’t be.

Of course, none of that necessarily means that it was right or acceptable for OpenAI to fire these employees. But I’ll withhold judgment on that until we know more about what happened.

Based on what’s known so far, the researchers likely wouldn’t qualify for legal whistleblower protection, as Bullock says. But the firings still put OpenAI in an awkward spot. The company is drawing a line between sanctioned and unsanctioned sharing with outside safety groups at the same time the industry is, slowly, inviting those groups in.

Last month, Anthropic said it would let outside evaluators like METR verify its safety practices and assess its models. OpenAI opened its own doors to METR and Redwood Research for six days after its agents hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI was also criticized at the time for the lack of time and access it granted METR to investigate the hack, and Korbak, one of the fired researchers, says he was the company’s technical contact for that investigation.

Regulators are also beginning to demand more transparency and responsibility from the labs. In September, for example, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said OpenAI’s management needed to take responsibility for the recent agent hacks. Last week, California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI as part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks related to its AI models. The FTC also launched an investigation into AI safety practices at Anthropic and OpenAI.

And, also last week, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI, and Nvidia signed a voluntary White House pact that commits them to partnering with independent external auditors.

The firings also weren’t the only safety departure at OpenAI last week. David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches, resigned and published an essay in The Atlantic arguing the company’s culture is broken. Robinson argued that AI companies can’t be relied on to police themselves, and that real pressure to prioritize safety has to come from outside.

All of this makes the recent terminations tricky for OpenAI and shows that safety disclosures are still very much at the whims of the labs. Right now, in part because of a lack of government intervention, the companies are the only ones deciding what the public knows about these hacks.

The biggest controversy came in June, when Anthropic began mandating a 30-day retention policy for all chats with its most powerful AI models, Fable and Mythos. Many companies had an “almost allergic reaction” to this, says a source who advises clients on becoming AI-native, speaking under the condition of anonymity because his company works closely with Anthropic. “The industry at large totally rejected it, and was pretty angry about it.”

A month later, both Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Palantir CEO Alex Karp warned companies against relying on AI models from frontier AI companies, saying that they risked having the IP siphoned off. “You essentially pay for intelligence twice, once with money, and again with something even more valuable: the proprietary knowledge you must reveal to make that intelligence useful,” Nadella said. OpenAI and Anthropic have stated they do not train their models on enterprise data.

Still, many data security experts say the AI companies may have subtler ways to glean insights about how their customers’ operate that can be used to improve future AI models, without having to train directly on the data the models’ are processing. “From a business standpoint, the risk of any of that data being trained on an AI model is unacceptable,” Rob Gregory, Vice President and Chief Information Security Officer at Optiv, a B2B cybersecurity advisory company, tells Fortune. “We’re at a very interesting crossroad.”

The latest string of “rogue AI” incidents have heightened fears that the latest models will either scrape data, or publish it for the world to see, without the business’ permission.

Given these concerns, companies are looking to diversify their AI usage, and reduce their dependency on the leading AI companies. The term du jour for this is “sovereign AI,” referring to a company’s ability to control its own “AI stack”—everything from owning the chips on which AI workloads run, to setting up proprietary cloud infrastructure, to using open source models that a company can download and run in their own cloud environments.

Sovereign AI is a term that has historically been associated with governments, but this year its usage has bled into the corporate world.

“Data sovereignty is something we’re talking a lot about,” said Brooke Hopkins, founder of voice AI company Coval. Dutta also said sovereign AI has “been a large topic of conversation for us over the past few months.”

The problem is that running open source AI models requires more technical expertise and, in some cases, may also mean that companies are not getting the cutting-edge capabilities, in areas such as coding or financial analysis, that some of the products from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google offer. “You’re trading control for responsibility, right?” Gregory said. “Because there is a significant amount of responsibility when you bring that internally.”

OpenAI and Anthropic are still earning trust

Anthropic and OpenAI are competing directly to win over business customers, and keep the ones they have from either switching companies or seeking open source alternatives.

OpenAI saw an opening to win customers after Anthropic’s data retention announcement, and in an August 19 blog post reiterated that it offers full ZDR for enterprise customers, while also previewing a new feature called Private Safety Processing (PSP). PSP adds a data storage element to ZDR, while also offering a system in which customers can store data in their own cloud, rather than on OpenAI’s servers.

Anthropic responded on Sept. 1 with a new, similar version of ZDR that also offers businesses a way to store their data on their own cloud accounts—not Anthropic’s. But has the damage already been done? After the company announced its 30-day retention policy, businesses like Booz Allen decided to restrict their teams’ use of its Fable model, The Information reported.

Another common route for businesses to use leading models from these companies is through Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock is an entrypoint for companies to access multiple AI models, without the providers seeing their data. It’s one of the fastest growing AWS products of all time, with customer spend growing 170% in Q1, and nearly 80% adoption by the Fortune 100.

“Amazon is like, ‘You don’t have to trust the frontier labs,’” said Randall Hunt, chief technology officer at Caylent, an AWS advisory company. “It’s a more established company people have been using for decades.”

Open models require more oversight—and obtaining GPUs

Many companies are adopting a “hybrid model,” Gregory said, meaning they are using some combination of closed models and open source models.

“Sovereign AI basically enables you to say, ‘Okay, I will continue to partner with OpenAI and Anthropic for some things, but maybe here’s another set of use cases that I want to use open source models for on prem,” Dutta added.

But this requires companies themselves to secure the models and implement them responsibly. Glen Wise, CEO and co-founder of Cinder, which makes software that helps detect and remediate model abuse, has seen a spike in inbound customer requests since Anthropic announced Fable would not have ZDR. “We’ve already been working with the main model creators, but in the past few weeks we have started getting requests from regular companies that are trying to figure out how to deploy open models,” Wise said.

Businesses with particularly sensitive data, such as health records, are not shying away from these added responsibilities, and some are even taking it a step further by running open models on their own GPUs, essentially becoming miniature data center owners. Payroll company Paycom told Fortune it has taken this approach because of the sensitive customer data and financial information it handles.

This is still relatively uncommon, but some people think it will prove to be the smartest long-term strategy.

“There’s a big shift going on, whereas in the past 25 years, [businesses would] pick your hyper-scalers, and then just let them take care of all things compute,” said Dan Wright, the founder and CEO of Armada, which makes portable data centers and will provide the infrastructure for Palantir and Nvidia’s forthcoming joint offering to help other businesses adopt fully sovereign AI. Crusoe,another company that has pivoted from building massive data centers to focusing on tiny ones. It was recently valued at $31 billion in a venture capital round earlier this month, according to the Wall Street Journal. “This is very much the direction the market is going,” Wright said.

But not every company is as anxious about data and IP leaking to the AI companies. “While I need to be paranoid about my IP, I trust the big AI companies are going to do the right thing because we’re both on the line to make sure it’s secure,” said Dan Cane, co-CEO of ModMed.

name: Microsoft
title: Satya Nadella reinvented Microsoft once. Can he do it again in the AI era? - CNBC
description:
Sven Hoppe | Picture Alliance | Getty Images On a sunny day in Seattle in late September, about 50 executives representing large Microsoft customers had a rare opportunity.
For longtime Microsoft investors, Nadella has a solid track record when it comes to navigating industry shifts.
"GitHub Copilot went out and learned lessons," said Kyle Daigle, the unit's operating chief, in an interview.
At the September Copilot event, Nadella stood before a slide declaring that Copilot could connect to "every model," with the Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Microsoft AI logos.
While Nadella earned investor trust in reviving Microsoft once, he can't afford to let the company become an also-ran in AI.
text:
Sven Hoppe | Picture Alliance | Getty Images

On a sunny day in Seattle in late September, about 50 executives representing large Microsoft customers had a rare opportunity. They could ask anything of CEO Satya Nadella.

One attendee wanted to know what Microsoft could do to help companies adapt to the artificial intelligence age. Nadella responded by emphasizing the importance of "diffusion inside the enterprise," meaning AI tools need to be widely deployed.

"Like all things, change is always bottom up, top down, and middle up," said Nadella, sporting a tight black crewneck and dark gray slacks, as he strode across the stage at the downtown Paccar Pavilion.

For the 59-year-old Nadella, who's spent over half his life at Microsoft, the gathering landed at a pivotal moment, as the software giant tries to magnify its role in the AI boom. Of late, Nadella has been inserting himself more into the AI discourse, posting on X last month about the need for "deliberate pacing" in model development, and days later addressing safety fears at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles.

Despite its almost $4 trillion market cap, Microsoft has yet to break out as an AI leader. Nvidia dominates in AI chips, Anthropic and OpenAI boast the foremost models, Meta just released the first mass-market personal agent, and Google's Gemini-powered services are popular with businesses and consumers.

Microsoft was aggressively early to AI through an investment in OpenAI, but that alliance has frayed. While the software giant has a big business in renting out chips for AI developers through its Azure cloud, its Copilot technology isn't pervasive in the workplace, and its proprietary AI models remain niche.

The company is hosting a Windows and Surface event in San Francisco on Wednesday, describing it in an invitation as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC."

Wall Street is lukewarm on the story. Even factoring in a sharp third-quarter rally, the stock is trailing its megacap peers and the broader Nasdaq this year, up just 7% as of Friday's close. Microsoft hasn't beaten the S&P 500 in a calendar year since 2023.

Stock Chart IconStock chart icon

Tiffany Wade, co-portfolio manager at Microsoft shareholder Columbia Threadneedle, said there are a lot of unknowns about Copilot, which is the centerpiece of Nadella's AI strategy.

"I think there needs to be a little bit more maturity of the product before we figure out actually what the best solution or what pricing is," Wade said in an interview.

For longtime Microsoft investors, Nadella has a solid track record when it comes to navigating industry shifts. He was named CEO in 2014, succeeding Steve Ballmer, who had presided over a roughly 33% drop in the stock price during his 14-year tenure, as Microsoft slipped into the beleaguered category of legacy software.

Nadella proceeded to turn Microsoft into a cloud powerhouse. He tossed aside perpetual Office software licenses and pushed the company into subscription-based software-as-a-service offerings alongside Azure infrastructure. And he permitted customers to integrate products from bitter rivals like Oracle and Salesforce , rather than insisting on a pure Microsoft stack.

Trained as an electrical engineer and computer scientist, Nadella became a savvy dealmaker, expanding Microsoft through acquisitions of "Minecraft"-maker Mojang, business social network LinkedIn and code-sharing service GitHub.

In recent months, Nadella has acknowledged to investors that he's got to change the business model yet again, this time to reflect the AI-fueled move toward consumption-based pricing. That means becoming a vendor of large volumes of tokens, which measure computing usage and represent the currency of the AI economy.

Success would mean "further expanding our TAM," Nadella said on Microsoft's July earnings call, adopting the acronym for total addressable market.

Much of the growth story Nadella preaches involves the production of software. Develop more code and do it faster, boosted by the latest and greatest AI tools.

"We went from the code assist to the agentic coding to software factory all within one year," Nadella said at the customer gathering late last month.

Now he wants to see Microsoft clients open their own software factories, spending more along the way to help churn out code. He's also hoping to empower non-technical knowledge workers. Some of Nadella's lieutenants at the event unveiled a Copilot "super app" that can perform increasingly complex tasks, generate simple applications and function as a virtual teammate.

Nadella had a preview of what was coming.

Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, when the company was still a fledgling lab. In 2021, a year before ChatGPT launched, Microsoft and OpenAI collaborated to release GitHub Copilot, a tool that could write parts of applications and websites based on vast swaths of public source code.

They'd created an early sensation. But as the generative AI market took off, developers moved to products from AI-native startups like Cursor, now owned by SpaceX , and Anthropic, which rolled out Claude Code.

'Learned lessons'

Microsoft's sluggishness in keeping up with the rapid changes cost GitHub market share.

Earlier this year, Microsoft adjusted the pricing for the coding tool to align more with computing demand. Some customers initially balked, but by July the company said it had racked up 50 million users, up from 26 million last October, meaning that one in five on GitHub were on board.

Nadella said on the July earnings call that GitHub Copilot sales growth accelerated 60% from the previous quarter, with "significant consumption revenue after the new model went into effect."

"GitHub Copilot went out and learned lessons," said Kyle Daigle, the unit's operating chief, in an interview.

Daigle said GitHub employees shared their lessons with other teams at Microsoft that are eyeing consumption-based pricing schemes.

Hayete Gallot, Microsoft's executive vice president for security products, said the company will charge clients according to how intensely they use the technology.

"I always say to my team, when customers consume, it means we add value. And for me, the truth starts with customers," Gallot said. "If they don't consume, it means we're not giving value."

Currently, Microsoft's enterprise portfolio is reliant on subscriptions. For its core Microsoft 365 productivity suite, which includes Word, Excel and Teams, customers sign up for years at a time, and Copilot costs an extra $30 per person each month. Microsoft has 30 million Copilot seats. The commercial Office 365 base exceeds 450 million.

Stephen Brashear | Getty Images News | Getty Images

One area of uncertainty in Microsoft's AI roadmap revolves around Mustafa Suleyman.

Suleyman previously co-founded AI lab DeepMind, which Google bought in 2014. Nadella hired him in 2024 to lead AI initiatives as Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI was cooling.

Last year, Microsoft lost its status as OpenAI's exclusive cloud provider, and this year its license on OpenAI intellectual property became non-exclusive. That left the software company with a massive investment in the AI lab but less preferential treatment. Microsoft said in April that it continues to serve as OpenAI's "primary cloud partner."

Suleyman's group has rolled out models for coding, image generation and reasoning. This week he boasted on X that a new speech-to-text model was "the most accurate real time transcription model in the world... #1 !!!" But for raw digital intellect, the team has yet to rival Anthropic or OpenAI, according to independent leaderboards.

Microsoft executives say there are benefits to having model and application development under the same roof. The group building Teams and other Office productivity apps has seen higher performance from Suleyman's transcription models at a lower price, and engineers get clear feedback as they build out products, said Executive Vice President Charles Lamanna.

"The collaboration is much tighter with Mustafa," he said.

Suleyman maintains a high profile at Microsoft, but his responsibilities have shifted. In March, Microsoft announced that it was bringing together the engineering groups for its commercial and consumer Copilot assistants, as adoption had been sluggish. Jacob Andreou was promoted to executive vice president for Copilot experience, and Suleyman was charged with focusing on model development.

Nadella, meanwhile, has been downplaying the importance of world-beating models in isolation.

"In my view, our priority has to be building a frontier ecosystem, not just a frontier model, so value flows broadly across every company, every industry, and every country," he wrote in a post on his SN Scratchpad website in June.

At the September Copilot event, Nadella stood before a slide declaring that Copilot could connect to "every model," with the Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Microsoft AI logos.

Fixing the economics

Increasingly, Microsoft is finding the model leaders encroaching on its turf, as they release products for cybersecurity, customer service and other functions.

In January, as Anthropic's Claude Code was building momentum, Microsoft executives were impressed with its ability to tap a bevy of tools to get things done, said Jared Spataro, Microsoft's marketing chief for AI at work. Microsoft was losing deals to Anthropic, promoting a close study of a rising competitor, said a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named due to confidentiality.

A Microsoft spokesperson declined to comment.

Spataro said the company sensed a need to change the mechanics.

"It became very clear to us at that moment. Like, oh wow, the economics are not going to be such that we're going to be able to offer now the best outcome within a fixed price per user per month," Spataro said. "We realized that we needed to start to think about the business model."

The company got cracking on a more comprehensive approach to consumption-based pricing that it calls usage-based billing, or UBB. The first UBB product was Copilot Cowork, which accepts large productivity assignments and shows its progress, Spataro said.

Nadella said on the July earnings call that "earlier this month, we added usage-based billing to Cowork with thousands of customers already paying for and actively using it."

Courtesy: Microsoft

Derrick Wood, an analyst at Cowen, said it was a strong signal.

"It may have the effect of what we saw when Claude Code, for example, shifted to consumption pricing, and you saw token bills go significantly higher," said Wood, who recommends buying Microsoft shares. "There's definitely the possibility for that to happen with Cowork."

Nadella is a user. On a podcast recorded after the September event, he said he can ask Cowork to prepare a supply chain optimization spreadsheet showing multiple scenarios.

"It'll create a fantastic artifact," he said.

David Berry, a vice president at advisory group Directions on Microsoft, said budget-conscious IT executives aren't all ready to take the Cowork plunge.

"There's a very real concern that you just kind of turn it on and people are going to start draining the bank," Berry said. "There's no way to determine if people are actually getting any benefit from it."

With the ChatGPT era nearing its four-year anniversary, Microsoft is still looking for a smash hit, whether at the model or application layer. While Nadella earned investor trust in reviving Microsoft once, he can't afford to let the company become an also-ran in AI.

Berry said he still sees Nadella as the right person to command the ship.

"He seems to be able to handle the situations or identify the situations and come up with a plan to change and evolve the business," he said. "The challenge is we're facing a lot more of the unknowns in a sense with AI, so it's a lot of different market dynamics going on, but he seems to have a plan, and he's working the plan."

In Seattle, Nadella ended his response to the transformation question by saying that those at the top of organizations play a key role.

"Leaders who are hands-on are able to change," he said. "Otherwise, they're all from press event to press event, right?"

He added, "It's kind of like you've got to be in it."

name: Air Liquide
title: Carbon Capture Is Coming For Cement's CO2 Emissions
description:
Carbon capture isn’t just an option for cement – it’s the only way to tackle the industry’s fundamental chemistry problem.
From Brevik to the Next Generation of Cement CCS Brevik matters because it proved cement CCS can survive contact with commercial reality.
That hard floor is why carbon capture sits at the center of long-term decarbonization planning.
The question is no longer if carbon capture is necessary, but how: Which capture specs fit which assets?
Although the winning technology stack hasn’t been finalized, for cement’s hardest-to-abate emissions, carbon capture has officially moved from a prospective fix to an operational imperative.
text:
Carbon capture isn’t just an option for cement – it’s the only way to tackle the industry’s fundamental chemistry problem.

In 2026, the conversation among producers has shifted from asking if the technology works to figuring out which business models and tech stacks can scale fast enough.

Responsible for roughly 8% of global CO2 emissions, with production hitting 4 billion tons in 2024, per LeadIT, cement remains one of the hardest industrial sectors to abate. The core issue isn’t energy use; it’s chemistry. Making conventional Portland cement requires heating limestone to extreme temperatures, triggering calcination and releasing CO2 directly from the rock itself.

Switching kilns to alternative fuels, boosting efficiency, or running on clean power trims operational footprint, but it can’t stop the chemical release of CO2​. Other strategies help at the margins: cutting clinker ratios, blending in supplementary materials, or leaning into alternatives like calcined clay, which is gaining real momentum across multiple continents.

Yet no silver-bullet technology can replace traditional cement production at global scale today.

That’s where carbon capture steps in.

Instead of trying to re-engineer limestone, point-source capture traps flue emissions before they reach the atmosphere, directing concentrated CO2​ toward permanent storage or utilization. For the sector’s hardest-to-avoid emissions, point-source capture is fast becoming a baseline necessity.

From Brevik to the Next Generation of Cement CCS

Brevik matters because it proved cement CCS can survive contact with commercial reality.

Integrated directly into Heidelberg Materials‘ Norwegian facility, the plant captures roughly 400,000 tons of CO2​ annually. The captured gas is liquefied, shipped, and ultimately injected into deep saline aquifers beneath the North Sea via the Northern Lights network.

Crucially, Brevik demonstrated something beyond capture mechanics: the viability of a complete, cross-border CO2​ value chain. Capturing flue gas is only step one. Conditioning, transporting, and permanently sequestering it is where the real complexity lies.

Relevant: CURA Raises $10M To Scale Cement Decarbonization Tech

Heidelberg Materials is already doubling down on this playbook.

Its Padeswood project in North Wales reached FID in 2025 with a target to capture 800,000 tons of CO2​ per year, effectively wiping out the plant’s net footprint. Scheduled for commissioning in 2029, Padeswood will pipe its captured gas directly to offshore storage in Liverpool Bay via the HyNet cluster.

Padeswood signals the industry’s broader direction: moving past first-of-a-kind demonstrations and designing commercial-scale assets built for maximum capture rates.

Holcim Is Testing Multiple Answers to the Same Problem

Few majors are hedging their bets quite like Holcim. The building materials giant is treating its asset base as a global proving ground, testing competing capture technologies to see which survive commercial deployment.

In January 2026, Holcim backed up this strategy by taking an equity stake in Norwegian capture company Capsol Technologies, following successful trials of Capsol’s post-combustion unit at the Dotternhausen plant in Germany.

Months later, Holcim partnered with Air Liquide to launch an industrial-scale pilot at its CaptureLab site in France. Deploying Air Liquide’s Cryocap FG tech built specifically for cement flue gas, the pilot targets one of CCS’s dirtiest bottlenecks: cleaning and conditioning harsh industrial flue streams prior to separation.

While the French pilot isn’t designed as a commercial unit, its operational data is feeding directly into larger industrial assets.

The primary beneficiary is Holcim and Air Liquide’s flagship GO4ZERO project in Obourg, Belgium. The facility pairs an oxyfuel-ready clinker line with Cryocap OXY technology, substituting pure oxygen for ambient air during combustion to yield a dense, easily separated CO2​ stream. The project targets a staggering 1.1 million tons of annual CO2​ capture capacity.

Meanwhile, Holcim is exploring entirely different storage paradigms in the Middle East.

In August, Holcim UAE and carbon mineralization firm 44.01 launched a continuous capture and underground mineralization setup at the Fujairah plant. Capturing 4 to 4.5 tons of CO2​ daily, the system skips traditional pipeline transport entirely, injecting the gas straight into local ultramafic rock formations where it permanently turns into solid stone.

The Scale Problem

This wave of project activity is promising, but it also lays bare the vast gap between pilot wins and global industrial reality.

LeadIT’s Green Cement Technology Tracker currently monitors over 175 projects worldwide, spanning CCUS and calcined clay. The organization projects roughly 38 cement CCS facilities will be operational by 2035.

The catch? Even if every single planned facility comes online on schedule, LeadIT estimates they will capture less than 2% of total global cement emissions by 2035.

Scaling CCS isn’t about celebrating a dozen marquee assets – it requires retrofitting or building hundreds, if not thousands, of heavy industrial facilities.

The CO2 Infrastructure Challenge

Once CO2​ leaves a cement kiln, logistics take over. Depending on location, that means high-pressure pipelines, specialized marine transport, or direct access to localized storage geology.

Brevik relies on liquefaction and maritime transport into the Northern Lights hub. Padeswood relies on direct pipeline access to offshore storage in Liverpool Bay. Obourg is building around a midstream model that hinges on Belgium’s emerging cross-border transport and export trunklines.

These facilities highlight a hard truth: cement CCS isn’t just a cement problem. A producer can install state-of-the-art capture equipment, but without shared transport infrastructure and certified storage sinks, the asset is useless.

Who Pays for Cement CCS?

Point-source capture is expensive, and capital expenditure doesn’t end at the absorber column. Producers must fund extensive plant modifications, compression hardware, midstream tariffs, and long-term storage fees.

The IEA projects that early-mover plants producing near-zero-emissions cement via CCS will face production costs 75% to 150% higher than traditional facilities, depending on local energy and transport economics.

Which brings us to the core commercial bottleneck: who absorbs that premium?

Relevant: Cool Planet Officially Opens Carbon Capture Plant At Holcim Facility

For now, direct government grants and capital subsidies are carrying flagship projects across the finish line. Over time, rising carbon pricing could tip the scales by penalizing unabated production.

Concurrently, producers are testing buy-side appetite for low-carbon products. Heidelberg Materials is marketing green tons directly through its evoZero brand, while Holcim continues expanding its low-carbon product lines.

Whether these early commercial offerings turn into broad market signals depends on how aggressively carbon prices rise, how government policy evolves, who funds shared midstream infrastructure, and whether off-takers are willing to pay a real green premium for decarbonized materials.

Carbon Capture Is Not the Whole Cement Solution

The momentum behind CCS shouldn’t drown out complementary decarbonization levers.

Reducing clinker ratios, scaling supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), co-processing alternative fuels, driving thermal efficiency, and formulating novel binders remain essential.

These aren’t competing strategies, they are prerequisites.

The IEA’s cement roadmap treats material efficiency, alternative fuels, and carbon capture as stacked solutions. The economic logic is simple: every ton of CO2​ eliminated upfront is a ton you don’t have to pay to capture, transport, and bury.

Yet even after maximizing efficiency and material substitution, unavoidable process emissions from calcination remain. That hard floor is why carbon capture sits at the center of long-term decarbonization planning.

From Demonstration to Deployment

Cement CCS has crossed an important threshold.

Brevik proved that point-source capture works on an operating plant. Padeswood is establishing the blueprint for higher capture rates. Holcim is field-testing diverse tech stacks across Europe and the Middle East, while developers advance assets across North America and Asia.

Now, the sector faces an entirely different challenge: It must scale midstream transport, secure long-term geological sinks, compress unit economics, and cultivate real market demand for green cement.

For cement executives, the strategic mandate has evolved. The question is no longer if carbon capture is necessary, but how: Which capture specs fit which assets? Where is the nearest storage sink? Who builds the shared pipeline networks? And which off-takers will step up to pay for cement that leaves its chemical footprint behind?

Although the winning technology stack hasn’t been finalized, for cement’s hardest-to-abate emissions, carbon capture has officially moved from a prospective fix to an operational imperative.

GLOBAL NEWS French Bond Yields Stay Elevated, Treasury Yields Ease French government bond yields rose on Monday, staying at elevated levels not far below Friday's multiyear highs, amid building concerns over the country's indebtness.
text:
MARKET WRAPS

Stocks:

European shares were largely up Monday while the euro fell weighed by worries that French fiscal stress would spread elsewhere on the continent.

French government bond yields rose on Monday, staying at elevated levels not far below Friday's multiyear highs.

"We suspect that bond market nervousness will remain in the near term," Investec said.

Meanwhile, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called fresh parliamentary elections for next month after protests against high housing costs, adding to the instability rocking European politics.

Oil prices fell, but remained over $100 a barrel, as recovering Middle East crude exports and the release of oil stocks by the Group of Seven eased concerns over supplies. President Trump also ruled out a diesel export ban, which would have tightened international products markets.

The recent rise in energy prices may cool demand in the eurozone through a variety of channels that would limit the need for rate rises to contain inflation, European Central Bank Chief Economist Philip Lane said Monday.

ING said the ECB has a difficult job in terms of "talking tough to keep a lid on inflation, while at the same time being expected to step in at some point should the French debt selloff get out of hand."

Looking ahead this week, Eurozone economic data due will be watched against the backdrop of bond-market worries. Investors will also watch for the European Central Bank's accounts of its September meeting due on Thursday for clues on when rates could rise again.

U.S. Markets:

Stock futures were lower Monday as investors continued to consider heightened bond yields.

Investors will also be keeping an eye on the two service purchasing managers indexes set for release, with the S&P Global version due at 2:45 p.m. GMT and the Institute for Supply Management's at 3 p.m. GMT.

Forex:

The euro fell to a 16-month low against the dollar, weighed by France's fiscal woes. The currency's decline over the past days reflects the cyclical outperformance of the U.S. versus the rest of the world, and in particular versus the euroarea economy, said Bank J. Safra Sarasin.

The dollar rose, hovering close to a near 18-month peak reached overnight against a basket of currencies and supported by expectations for interest-rate rises and French fiscal concerns.

The greenback could extend gains against the euro if the recent widening in the OAT-Bund spread persists, OCBC said. "Wider peripheral spreads tend to tighten eurozone financial conditions and weigh on [euro] sentiment," it added.

Bonds:

French government bond yields were up, albeit below Friday's multiyear highs, due to concerns about France's fiscal situation, risks that parliament might not agree on the government's budget, and a looming election next year.

Spanish 10-year government bond yields trade steady, underperforming their German peers whose yields fell.

Treasury yields fell after U.S. nonfarm payrolls rose just 29,000 and the unemployment rate increased to 4.2% in September, according the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday.

Higher bond yields are hitting rate-sensitive sectors first, Saxo Markets said. Utilities and real estate sectors face higher refinancing costs and stronger competition from bonds, it added.

Energy:

Front-month Brent crude was down 0.9%, while WTI futures declined 1.5%.

Metals:

Gold prices rose after recent soft U.S. economic data sharply lowered expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in October, though a stronger dollar limited gains.

EMEA HEADLINES

Schneider Electric to Buy Software Maker PTC for $22.6 Billion

France's Schneider Electric agreed to buy PTC in an all-cash deal that values the U.S. industrial-software maker at $22.6 billion, moving to prepare its portfolio for industrial artificial intelligence.

Schneider said Monday that it offered $205 a share in cash for PTC, a 42% premium to its last closing price. PTC's board decided to recommend that the company's shareholders approve the deal.

Akzo Nobel to Sell Southeast Asia Decorative Paints Business for $1.35 Billion

Akzo Nobel has agreed to sell its decorative paints business in Southeast Asia to Nippon Paint at an enterprise value of $1.35 billion.

The Dutch paint company said Monday that net cash proceeds after taxes and minority partners are expected to be about $1 billion.

Air Liquide Targets Sales, Margin Growth Under 2030 Plan

Air Liquide said it is targeting sales growth and higher margins under a new strategic plan through 2030.

The industrial gasses company said Monday that it wants to grow net earnings per share by a compound annual growth rate of 10% over the period, from the 6.1 euros it reported for 2025.

Robotics Startup RobCo Hits $1 Billion Valuation

German robotics startup RobCo has sold shares in a deal that values the company at more than $1 billion-double the level hit earlier this year-highlighting investor enthusiasm for physical AI systems.

The company makes autonomous industrial robots aimed at automating repetitive manual tasks like stacking pallets and weighing raw materials. Its new flagship product is a two-armed, self-learning robot called Alfie that is designed to mimic a human working on a factory floor.

GLOBAL NEWS

French Bond Yields Stay Elevated, Treasury Yields Ease

French government bond yields rose on Monday, staying at elevated levels not far below Friday's multiyear highs, amid building concerns over the country's indebtness.

Treasury yields eased meanwhile after weaker-than-expected U.S. nonfarm payrolls data caused markets to trim expectations for another U.S. interest-rate increase in October.

Oil Prices Fall as G-7 Plans Crude, Diesel Release But Hormuz Shipping Risks Persist

Oil prices fell Monday as traders weighed a planned release of emergency oil and diesel stocks by the Group of Seven countries against renewed attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and persistent Middle East supply risks.

December Brent crude futures fell 0.7% to $101.59 a barrel, while December West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 1% to $88.54 a barrel.

ECB's Lane Sees 'Demand Destruction' Muting Energy Impact On Inflation

The recent rise in energy prices may cool demand in the eurozone through a variety of channels that would limit the need for rate rises to contain inflation, European Central Bank Chief Economist Philip Lane said Monday.

The ECB last month raised its key interest rate for the second time since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran in late February. Investors expect to see further increases in borrowing costs following data released last week that showed eurozone inflation reached a three-year high in September.

FBI Arrests Alleged Chinese Agent Accused of Spying on Son of Taiwan Leader

The FBI arrested a California realtor on Sunday on charges of acting as an unregistered agent of China, accusing her of spying on a son of Taiwan's president under the direction of Chinese officials.

The alleged foreign agent, Wanying Zhang, a 34-year-old resident of Irvine, Calif., was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport before she could board a flight to Shanghai, U.S. authorities said.

Spain's Prime Minister Sanchez Calls Snap Elections After Housing Protests

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called fresh parliamentary elections for next month after protests against high housing costs, adding to the instability rocking European politics.

The socialist leader's move comes after a key piece of housing legislation offering more support to renters was rejected by lawmakers on Friday, demonstrating the fragility of the premier's mandate. Sanchez began a new term as head of the eurozone's fourth-largest economy in 2023 but lacks a parliamentary majority.

Flávio Bolsonaro Surges Past Lula, Setting Up a Bitter Brazil Election Runoff

SÃO PAULO-Flávio Bolsonaro dealt President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a bruising first-round defeat Sunday, finishing ahead of the leftist leader and putting Brazil's right within reach of taking back power in Latin America's largest nation.

Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator and the eldest son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, received 47.3% of votes, short of the 50% needed for an outright victory, while da Silva got just 44.8% with 98% counted late Sunday. Other right-wing candidates won a combined 5%, leaving the 80-year-old incumbent fighting for his political survival ahead of the Oct. 25 runoff.

Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit

DUBAI-Before Hamam al-Hammami stood behind his captain on FlyDubai Flight 1073 and raised an emergency ax to begin the assault that nearly brought down the plane, there had been ample opportunity for authorities in three countries to keep him from getting anywhere near that cockpit.

Oman had scrutinized his online habits and decided he showed too much interest in radical ideology to trust as a pilot at state carrier Oman Air, where he worked. They banned him from flying, sent him to a deradicalization program and put him in a desk job but didn't flag their concerns more broadly, people familiar with the matter said.

title: How AI is transforming biopharma manufacturing facilities of the future
description:
For designers, builders and facility owners, the question is no longer whether AI will reshape pharmaceutical manufacturing; it is how quickly facilities can adapt to support a faster, more dynamic development environment.
At the same time, pharmaceutical companies are investing heavily in United States manufacturing capacity, creating new opportunities for facility development and modernization.
Major organizations including Eli Lilly, Merck, AstraZeneca, Novo Nordisk, Genentech and Regeneron are increasing their United States investments amid a broader push to expand domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing.
Flexibility is becoming a core design requirement for manufacturing facilities While AI may help identify promising therapies faster, it does not eliminate uncertainty.
“We’re seeing more requests for pilot plants and process development facilities,” says Ahrendt.
text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is helping researchers identify promising drug candidates faster, reshaping how new pharmaceutical treatments move from development to clinical reality to patient delivery.

What once took years of laboratory research and validation can now happen in months, as AI-powered platforms identify promising drug candidates, analyze vast biological datasets and accelerate early-stage development.

As a result, pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies are advancing more therapies through the development pipeline than ever before. Recent breakthroughs are helping demonstrate that potential. In August 2026, Moderna and Merck announced positive late-stage trial results for a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, a milestone researchers say could open the door to similar therapies for a range of cancers.

The impact extends far beyond the research lab. For designers, builders and facility owners, the question is no longer whether AI will reshape pharmaceutical manufacturing; it is how quickly facilities can adapt to support a faster, more dynamic development environment.

Manufacturers now face growing pressure to bring new production capacity online faster while maintaining the stringent quality and regulatory standards the industry demands. At the same time, pharmaceutical companies are investing heavily in United States manufacturing capacity, creating new opportunities for facility development and modernization.

Major organizations including Eli Lilly, Merck, AstraZeneca, Novo Nordisk, Genentech and Regeneron are increasing their United States investments amid a broader push to expand domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing.

For designers, builders and facility owners, the question is no longer whether AI will reshape pharmaceutical manufacturing; it is how quickly facilities can adapt to support a faster, more dynamic development environment.

According to Andrew Ahrendt, director, national manufacturing at PCL Construction, three trends are having the greatest impact on biopharmaceutical facilities today: speed, flexibility and digital integration.

1. Speed is the new normal

Due to increased production speed, companies increasingly need to make facility decisions while pharmaceuticals are still being evaluated, creating new urgency around planning, permitting, design and construction.

“AI isn’t just accelerating the science,” says Ahrendt. “It’s compressing the entire capital planning cycle. Owners who used to have years to plan a facility are now making capacity decisions in a fraction of that time.”

That pressure is driving greater interest in modular construction, prefabricated utility systems and collaborative delivery models that allow multiple project activities to advance in parallel. Site selection, permitting, utility planning and process design increasingly occur concurrently rather than sequentially, helping owners move projects forward more quickly.

2. Flexibility is becoming a core design requirement for manufacturing facilities

While AI may help identify promising therapies faster, it does not eliminate uncertainty.

Manufacturers often do not know which products will ultimately succeed in clinical trials or reach commercial scale. As a result, facilities must be designed to adapt to changing production needs over time.

Many owners are prioritizing manufacturing environments that can accommodate multiple production strategies without extensive renovations. This includes modular scopes, expansion-ready utility infrastructure and “ballroom” manufacturing layouts, a pharmaceutical facility design approach that replaces a series of dedicated production rooms with a large, open manufacturing space where equipment can be added, removed or reconfigured as production needs change.

“We’re seeing more requests for pilot plants and process development facilities,” says Ahrendt. Pilot plants allow manufacturers to test and refine production processes before moving to commercial-scale manufacturing. “Owners are also asking for multi-product, flexible spaces rather than dedicated single-product lines because they don’t yet know which candidates in a larger pipeline will ultimately make it to commercial scale.”

This approach helps companies avoid investing in facilities or equipment they may not need while giving manufacturers more flexibility to respond to shifting market demand.

3. Building digital native facilities for biopharma

Technology tools that leverage AI — such as digital twins, predictive analytics and real-time data collection — are becoming increasingly important tools across the pharmaceutical industry. As manufacturers rely more heavily on these technologies to optimize processes, monitor equipment and improve operational performance, facility infrastructure must support those capabilities from the start.

That means data architecture and operational technology systems can no longer be treated as late-stage additions. Instead, digital scopes are moving earlier into the design process, influencing everything from facility layouts and utility systems to commissioning strategies and long-term asset management.

At PCL, digital twin-enabled documentation is already incorporated into project commissioning and closeout processes, helping owners begin operations with a more complete digital record of their facilities.

“Digital-native strategies are being deployed on all new facilities,” Ahrendt says. “Digital twins aren’t a nice-to-have anymore. Clients are depending on a data-rich handoff earlier and earlier in the project lifecycle and design construction partners need to be ready to deliver it.”

Keeping pace with innovation

Pharmaceutical manufacturers are expanding capacity, investing in digital technologies and rethinking how facilities are planned and operated.

The challenge now is ensuring facility development can keep pace with innovation.

text:
New framework delivers independent risk transparency for onchain investment vehicles, furthering S&P Global’s offerings across the DeFi space

SINGAPORE (OCTOBER 5, 2026) – S&P Global Ratings, a division of S&P Global (NYSE: SPGI), today launched its Vault Risk Assessment (VRA), a new analytical approach that delivers independent, forward-looking insights into the risks associated with digital asset lending vaults. The initiative brings institutional-grade transparency to the rapidly evolving digital asset ecosystem and supports informed decision-making for market participants.

What is a vault?

Digital asset lending vaults are investment vehicles that operate on a blockchain. They pool investor deposits and deploy them according to defined strategies, working much like managed fixed income funds. Total deposits in vaults reached US$10 billion as of September 2026, demonstrating rapid growth from US$1.5 billion two years earlier. While blockchain-based activity enables point-in-time transparency, strategy and risk disclosures for vaults have typically been limited.

The VRA Analytical Approach

S&P Global Ratings’ VRA is a forward-looking opinion about the overall relative risk of impairment to an investor’s position in a lending vault. The VRA provides a comprehensive view of a vault’s overall risk profile across six key risk factors:

Portfolio credit quality risk

Liquidity mismatch risk

Curator risk

Blockchain risk

Protocol risk

Vault security and governance risk

A VRA is not a credit rating and does not comment on yield levels. To read more about the VRA analytical approach, including the letter-based scale, visit spglobal.com/ratings/en/products/vault-risk-assessments.

“As digital assets continue to institutionalize, the demand for independent risk assessments that bridge traditional finance and decentralized innovation is paramount,” said Yann Le Pallec, President, S&P Global Ratings. “Our commitment to bringing transparency and rigorous analysis to all financial markets extends to this rapidly growing segment. The Vault Risk Assessment will empower investors and foster greater confidence and stability as capital flows into these new digital structures.”

The VRA analytical approach moves beyond transaction transparency to deliver essential risk transparency, enabling institutions to enhance their investment governance and selection processes and supporting broader adoption of the vault market.

“Digital asset vaults represent a significant evolution in onchain finance, offering new avenues for pooled investment and capital efficiency,” said James Wiemken, Executive Managing Director and Head of Global Ratings Services. “However, the inherent complexities and varying disclosure standards in this nascent market create a clear need for a standardized, independent risk perspective. The VRA fills this critical gap, providing market participants with the deep insights necessary to navigate vault investments with greater clarity and confidence.”

S&P Global Ratings will publish initial Vault Risk Assessments in future announcements.

A Strategic Focus on Digital Assets

S&P Global has established itself as a bridge between traditional finance and decentralized finance, leveraging its legacy of trusted risk frameworks, benchmarks, and analytical standards to support the institutionalization of digital asset markets.

Recent firsts include:

The industry’s first Stablecoin Stability Assessments

The first credit rating of a DeFi protocol (Sky Protocol)

Its first rating of a structured finance transaction backed by bitcoin: “Ledn”.

S&P DJI and Kaiko tokenize the iBoxx U.S. Treasuries Index on the blockchain.

In September 2026, S&P Global announced an agreement to acquire OpenZeppelin, the security standard for onchain finance. Earlier the same month, S&P Global led a strategic investment in Kaiko, the independent leader in digital asset market data, indices and data infrastructure. description:

text:
LONDON, Oct 4 (Reuters) - ​Revolut has ⁠risen to become Europe's most valuable startup and a challenge to centuries-old banking giants, ​having grown rapidly since it was launched just over a decade ago as a fintech promising cheaper forex fees.

Yet Revolut faces many hurdles itself, with the amount of revenue it extracts per customer a fraction of ​its ‌established competitors and a small lending business by industry standards.

A spokesperson for Revolut said in an email that the London-based company has a "diversified business model", earning its revenue from various products and services rather than lending.

"That means ⁠our growth depends on building things customers value, rather than on interest rates," the spokesperson said.

Here's Revolut's ⁠rise, in five charts:

GOING FOR GLOBAL

CEO Nik Storonsky has stressed he ​wants Revolut to be truly global, expanding into markets from Mexico to Australia.

The company has announced several new licences in recent weeks, as it aims to become one of only a handful of banks with retail operations spanning so much of the globe.

Meanwhile, some traditional lenders seen as global, including HSBC, are reducing their retail footprint.

Valued at $115 billion privately, Revolut is now worth more than ​Britain's Barclays and ‌France's Societe Generale as investors bet on its tech platform winning over more customers globally.

Revolut's 2025 pretax profit was £1.7 billion ($2.2 billion), a fraction of Barclays' £9 billion, but growing fast.

Paulo Macedo, CEO of Portugal's biggest bank, Caixa Geral de Depósitos, said in June that 2025 was the last year in which the 150-year-old bank would record higher profit than Revolut.

"When you go to Europe the bank CEOs there are talking about Revolut as their most important threat because of their aggressive marketing and growth," said Cihan Duran, director at S&P Global Ratings.

MARRED BY SETBACKS

In the US, ​where Revolut has a provisional license, it will face tougher competition, investors said.

"The US could be potentially the biggest growth for Revolut. But at the same time, the US is the most ‌competitive market," said Konstantin Sidorov, CEO of the London Technology Club, which invested in Revolut when it was valued at just $5.5 billion.

There have been setbacks, including a fine in Lithuania for failing to prevent money laundering. Revolut said an investigation had not identified any confirmed ‌instances of money laundering, adding that it had signed a settlement with the central bank and taken steps to resolve shortcomings.

And in September, Revolut accidentally sent customer data to hackers posing as government investigators. The company said its systems and customer funds were unaffected and it had contacted the "limited number of impacted individuals" to give support.

In 2024 and 2025, Revolut was the ​most-complained-about bank in Britain in fraud cases whereby customers are tricked into sending cash to scammers, Ombudsman data compiled by consumer advocacy firm Which? showed.

Revolut has previously said in response it takes fraud very seriously and has robust customer ‌protections in place.

CUSTOMERS HAVE SURGED

A striking measure of its growth is customer numbers.

In Ireland, for example, Revolut said that 80% of the adult population has a Revolut account.

Revolut's website shows it has 80 million customers, against 84 million for JPMorgan and 41 million for HSBC.

REVENUE-PER-CUSTOMER IS LOW

Revolut makes far less from each of its customers than traditional banks, a Reuters analysis of ⁠its figures shows. Average ⁠deposit balances are also much lower.

Lower per-customer revenue is in part because Revolut lends much less than traditional banks, instead ‌relying on fees such as card subscriptions.

With just £2.2 billion in loans at end-2025, Revolut's loan-to-deposit ratio of 6% compares with 55% for HSBC and 86% for Societe Generale.

Scaling its lending business will introduce risks including managing big and complex credit ​exposures, while entering fiercely competitive local mortgage markets will ​not be easy, analysts and investors said.

TOO FEW PRIMARY ACCOUNTS

Revolut has attracted customers with its easy-to-use app but executives acknowledge too few ‌use it as a primary bank account.

Revolut declined to comment in its latest results on how many customers did so in 2025, but said the figure was up 45% from a year ago.

This metric is a focus for Revolut's biggest backers.

Alex Immerman, an investor at Andreessen Horowitz, which is known as "a16z", told Reuters it was watching for primary-account adoption, as well as total customer balances.

Oct 5 (Reuters) - French industrial gases company Air Liquide on Monday launched a €4 billion ($4.5 billion) share buyback plan and said it aimed to raise its operating margin by 400 to 600 basis points by 2030 as part of a new mid-term strategy.

The buyback marks Air Liquide's first large-scale shareholder-return programme of its kind and is set to be completed by the end of 2028 alongside continued dividend growth. It forms part of a planned capital allocation of more than €40 billion for 2026-2030, of which over half is earmarked for industrial investment and acquisitions.

"Our profitability allows us to evolve our capital allocation beyond investments and acquisitions in our core businesses," CEO François Jackow said in a statement published ahead of the company's Capital Markets Day event.

Elliott Investment Management has reportedly built an undisclosed stake in Air Liquide and has been engaging with the French industrial-gases group for months, calling for margin improvements and a sharper focus on efficiency and capital returns.

Air Liquide, which supplies gases such as oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen to factories and hospitals, also forecast average sales growth of 5% a year, plus or minus 1 percentage point, through 2030.

text:
Foghorn Therapeutics Inc. (FHTX), a biotechnology company developing medicines targeting genetically determined dependencies in the chromatin regulatory system, said it will not advance FHD-909 program after reviewing data from its Phase 1 dose-escalation trial.

Further, the company also said it will halt further pursuit of the partnered selective SMARCA2 degrader program with Eli Lilly, effectively ending further collaboration activities between the companies.

FHD-909 (LY4050784) is an investigational, oral selective SMARCA2 (BRM) inhibitor designed to selectively inhibit SMARCA2 over the closely related SMARCA4 (BRG1).

The Phase 1 trial evaluated the drug in patients with SMARCA4-mutant advanced solid tumors, with non-small cell lung cancer as the primary target population.

According to Foghorn, the clinical data showed that the drug candidate selectively engaged the SMARCA2 target and had a favorable safety profile at exposures above preclinical targets.

However, the SMARCA2/4 synthetic-lethality strategy did not produce sufficient efficacy to justify further development. The company has not disclosed detailed Phase 1 efficacy results in the latest announcement.

Following the decision, the company plans to concentrate resources on its wholly owned pipeline, including selective EP300 and CBP degraders, a novel oral immunology and inflammation program, and its induced-proximity platform.

Additionally, the company also noted, it will reduce its workforce by approximately 40% as part of a broader organizational restructuring. Foghorn expects the pipeline prioritization and cost reductions to extend its cash runway into the second half of 2029.

Key pipeline milestones include IND filings targeted for 2027 for its selective EP300 degrader programs and novel immunology and inflammation program.

Following the announcement, Wedbush downgraded Foghorn to Neutral from Outperform and cut its price target to $2 from $10 on October 2.

Foghorn shares closed at $2.02, down 30.82%.

In the overnight market, stock is up 1.98% at $2.06.

text:
Japan's richest man and SoftBank Group founder Masayoshi Son, long regarded as one of artificial intelligence’s most vocal champions, has reportedly voiced sharp concern over the safety risks posed by rapidly advancing machines. According to a report by Bloomberg, speaking on the sidelines of the Science and Technology in Society forum in Kyoto, the Japanese billionaire warned that the exponential leap in AI capabilities leaves nations no choice but to foster mutual trust and govern the technology cooperatively. Son shared the stage with White House science and technology policy advisor Michael Kratsios, who unveiled a 17-nation initiative led by the United States aimed at deploying AI to speed up scientific discovery. Delegates from countries including Japan, South Korea, the UK, Germany, Singapore, and the United Arab Emirates appeared alongside Kratsios to endorse the pact. China was not among the initial signatories to the White House statement.

Masayoshi Son's 'rare warning' on the technology he has spent billions on

“We don’t have any more luxury of having human fight against humans,” Son said, emphasizing that countries must align to counter the far larger risks emerging from ultra-powerful systems. He warned that superintelligence landing in the wrong hands could quickly turn “super dangerous.” Son’s uncharacteristic caution comes amid escalating alarm following a string of security breaches linked to AI models in recent months, Bloomberg reported. The 69-year-old executive, who has steered roughly $65 billion of SoftBank capital into ChatGPT maker OpenAI, has historically championed the technology’s promise to uplift humanity while generating outsized returns. It has become one of the world's biggest backers of OpenAI under founder Son's push to make ⁠the Japanese conglomerate a dominant investor in AI. Son warned that the speed of progress will only accelerate. The underlying models driving today's chatbots—increasingly deployed to browse the web and write software using vast clusters of general-purpose chips—are poised to enter a third phase, enabling robots and machinery to interface directly with the physical world as soon as next year.

When SoftBank sold its entire stake in Nvidia to fund OpenAI

In November 2025, SoftBank announced that it has sold its entire stake in the US chipmaker Nvidia as the Japanese giant looks to capitalize on its “all in” bet on ChatGPT maker OpenAI. A month earlier in 2025, SoftBank sold 32.1 million shares of Nvidia. The company also sold part of its stake in T-Mobile for $9.17 billion to fund Sam Altman's company.

SoftBank makes final $30 billion payment to OpenAI

Last week, October 2026, SoftBank Group said that it has completed its $30 billion investment in ​OpenAI as part of its commitment ‌to the ChatGPT maker's last fundraising round. Earlier this year, OpenAI ​had secured $122 billion in commitments that ​valued the Sam Altman-led company at $852 ⁠billion.
